title: Partnering with AI: A Pedagogical Feedback System for LLM Integration into Programming Education
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how large language models (LLMs) can be used to generate pedagogically sound feedback for programming education, with a particular focus on whether LLM feedback can better align with teacher feedback strategies than typical one-size-fits-all prompting approaches. The authors argue that prior automated feedback systems often optimize technical correctness but neglect pedagogical principles such as mastery level and task progress.

To study this, the authors first conducted a preliminary semi-structured interview with one secondary-school computer science teacher to derive adaptation criteria for feedback. They then developed a web-based feedback system for Python programming that used multi-agent LLM prompts, validation agents, and pedagogically informed response policies. The system was evaluated with eight secondary-school computer science teachers in Germany through mixed-method semi-structured interviews, where teachers reviewed synthetic student requests, judged LLM-generated feedback on several quantitative scales, and discussed similarities and differences relative to their own feedback practices.

The study population consisted of in-service secondary-school computer science teachers teaching Python in German schools, with the evaluated scenarios framed around student programming tasks and help requests at secondary-school grade levels. The main conclusions are that teachers generally judged the LLM feedback to be pedagogically sound, comprehensive, and effective, especially for supporting high-performing students and detecting small code errors quickly. However, teachers also emphasized important limitations: the system could not adapt well to classroom context, could not observe real-time student work, and lacked interactive and visual teaching strategies. The paper concludes that LLMs can complement but not replace human teachers, and that pedagogically grounded prompting is preferable to generic prompting.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods teacher evaluation with a very small sample (n=8) and no randomized comparison or student learning outcome measure. It provides useful design evidence but limited causal credibility.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful benefits for feedback efficiency and instructional support, but the evidence is indirect and based on teacher judgments rather than measured student gains. The likely impact is therefore modest and still uncertain.

interventions.use_case: LLM-generated pedagogical feedback for secondary-school Python programming tasks, including adaptive hints, motivational prompts, and explanations tailored to student mastery level, task progress, and student input
multi-agent LLM system used as a conversational teacher/feedback partner to generate and validate student-facing responses in programming education

finding.finding_summary: In a mixed-method evaluation with eight secondary-school computer science teachers, the LLM feedback system was judged to be technically correct in 91.7% of reviewed cases (55/60 correct; 5/60 partially correct) and was rated as pedagogically sound, comprehensive, and effective. Mean ratings were 3.84/5 for pedagogical soundness (SD=1.10), 4.04/5 for comprehensiveness (SD=1.01), and 3.89/5 for effectiveness (SD=1.14).
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of correctness, pedagogical soundness, comprehensiveness, and effectiveness for programming feedback responses
finding.study_size: n=8 teachers; 60 sampled student requests/responses rated

finding.finding_summary: Teachers repeatedly reported that the system could provide instant, precise feedback and help identify small code errors faster than human teachers, suggesting workload and time-saving benefits. The study did not report a formal task-time effect size, but the qualitative evidence strongly favored faster feedback generation and parallel support for routine queries.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of speed, precision, and workload reduction in feedback provision
